newsitem.title: BANGLADESH: Bangladesh PM accuses detained leaders of sabotage.
newsitem.headline: Bangladesh PM accuses detained leaders of sabotage.

text.p: Bangladesh Prime Minister Sheikh Hasina on Monday defended the arrest of four key opposition leaders, accusing them of sabotaging her government.

"They were involved in sabotage. Maybe they themselves did not take part...but they had involvement. Definitely we have information (to support that)," she told a news conference on return from Pakistan after attending an extraordinary meeting of the Organisation of Islamic Conference (OIC). Police in a pre-dawn swoop on Thursday arrested the four leaders of the main opposition Bangladesh Nationalist Party (BNP) -- ex-ministers Khandaker Mosharraf Hossain, Abdul Mannan and Goyeswar Roy, and former mayor of Dhaka Mirza Abbas.
They were later sent to jail with a one-month detention order under a special security law. No formal charges have yet been laid against them.

The arrests were made ahead of Sunday's general strike called by the BNP, headed by former prime minister Begum Khaleda Zia, in its first major attempt to destabilise Hasina's nine-month old government.
Three people were killed and nearly 200 injured in sporadic strike-related violence across the country, police and witnesses said.

Hasina referred to the recent mysterious collapse of two supply towers of the national power grid, which left parts of northern Bangladesh in the dark for at least two days, and hinted that one among the arrested leaders was involved. She did not name the suspect.
The prime minister also indicated that the arrested opposition leaders could have had a hand in a recent strike in Chittagong port, which totally disrupted cargo handling for five days.
Hasina accused her political rival, Begum Khaleda Zia, of "creating trouble and tension without reason".
"What has led her to resort to such trouble-making on the street. What does she want?."
Hasina said she had had fruitful talks with Pakistan Prime Minister Nawaz Sharif on Monday on the vexed question of repatriating hundreds of thousands of stranded Pakistanis.
"We discussed about raising funds to finance their repatriation. Obviously these people will return to Pakistan," Hasina said.

Some 400,000 Urdu-speaking Moslems who opted for Pakistani citizenship after Bangladesh (formerly East Pakistan) seceded through a 1971 war of independence have since been left in squalid refugee camps in Bangladesh.

Hasina's remarks will be reassuring for the stranded Pakistanis or Biharis (so called because most of them had migrated to East Pakistan from India's Bihar state) as Bangladesh prepares to celebrate its 26th independence anniversary on Wednesday.
Bihari leader Mohammad Nasima Khan led an open-air prayer for Hasina and Nawaz Sharif in Dhaka on Saturday after the Bangladesh leader had left for Islamabad.
"The two could together change our fate. So we pray to Allah for both," Khan said.
